title: Purse

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Felt suits a purse because it holds its shape without a stiff lining and keeps its soft surface through years of being carried. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. A purse begins as a flat layered piece worked around a shape, so the body can come out with few seams. This page will introduce the purses made in the workshop, the sizes available, and what to ask about when ordering one piece or placing a wholesale enquiry from Nepal or abroad.

title: Bags

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. A felt bag is light for its size, soft against the body and strong enough for daily use when the wool has been worked densely. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. Larger pieces take longer to full evenly, and straps and handles are attached by hand once the body has dried. This introduction will describe the bag styles on offer, how much each one holds, the colours available, and how shops can ask about wholesale felt bags from Nepal.

title: Hats

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. A felt hat is shaped from a single seamless piece, which is what makes the material so well suited to headwear. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. The damp felt is then pulled over a form and left to dry until it keeps the curve of the crown. This introduction will explain the hat styles on offer, how sizes are measured, and how to enquire about colours or a batch order. Replace it with details from the people who make them.

title: Ornaments

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Small felt ornaments are made by needling or rolling wool into solid shapes, so they are light, soft to hold and hard to break. Details such as faces, leaves and tails are worked in by hand, which means no two turn out exactly alike. This introduction will describe the ornaments available, any seasonal ranges, how they are finished for hanging, and how shops can ask about buying assorted felt ornaments in quantity for retail or for gifts.

title: Key Rings and Key Chains

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. A felt key ring is small enough to be a first purchase and sturdy enough to be handled every day. Each shape starts as a tuft of wool rolled or needled until it is firm, then stitched to a metal ring by hand. Because they are quick to pack and easy to carry, they are a natural gift. This introduction will list the shapes available, how they are fastened, and how shops can ask about mixed batches of felt key chains.

title: Hotpot

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Thick wool felt is a natural insulator, and that is what makes it useful around hot cookware in the kitchen and at the table. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. Pieces for hot use need a denser felt than most others, so they are worked for longer before being dried and finished. This introduction will explain exactly what each hotpot piece is for, the sizes that suit different pots, how to clean them, and how to enquire about a larger order.

title: Tea Coaster

children.text: Sample text, to be replaced in the Studio. Tea coasters are among the simplest pieces to make well and the easiest way to bring handmade felt into a home. Felt is naturally absorbent and protects a table from the heat of a cup. Wool is laid out in thin layers, wetted with warm soapy water and worked by hand until the fibres lock together into dense cloth. Sheets are then cut or rolled into patterned rounds. This introduction will explain the shapes and colours on offer, whether sets can be mixed, and how cafes, hotels and gift shops can ask about wholesale felt tea coasters.

processSteps.title: Preparing the wool
processSteps.text: Sample text. Wool is sorted, cleaned, dyed and teased apart so that it lies evenly.

processSteps.title: Laying and wetting
processSteps.text: Sample text. Thin layers are laid out by hand, then wetted with warm soapy water.

processSteps.title: Rolling and shaping
processSteps.text: Sample text. Pressure and movement lock the fibres together into firm felt, which is shaped while damp.

processSteps.title: Drying and finishing
processSteps.text: Sample text. Pieces are dried, then trimmed, stitched and checked by hand.
